kurz: How to make decisions comparable when each of them only happens once.

bloecke.md:
Most money decisions happen exactly once. You do not buy a house a thousand times, and a severance payment is not negotiated every year. Nor can you try out the sale of a position in several variants at the same time. Nevertheless, such individual cases can only be compared with one another using probability theory. It translates an assessment such as “this could work out” into a number that can be set against another number.

The first step is to translate probabilities into frequencies, which demonstrably avoids errors. In 1983, Tversky and Kahneman showed with the so-called Linda problem that around 85% of respondents consider a more specific story more likely than the more general one in which it is contained. If the same question is asked in frequency format (“out of 100 people: how many?”), the error rate falls to about 20%. People cope better with frequencies than with percentages. You should therefore deliberately translate the assessment “this company has good prospects” into a frequency, for example “out of 100 companies in this situation, thirty make it”.

bloecke.formel: E = p1 × x1 + p2 × x2 + … + pn × xn
bloecke.erklaerung: The expected value is the sum of all possible outcomes weighted by their probabilities. It does not describe an outcome that occurs in any single case. It is the average you would see if the same decision were made very many times, each time independently.
variablen: Probability of outcome i; all p add up to 1
Outcome i, measured in euros or as a percentage of the stake
bloecke.beispiel: A stake in a company returns +200% with a probability of 30% and ends in a total loss with a probability of 70%. E = 0.30 × 200 + 0.70 × (−100) = 60 − 70 = −10%. Despite the chance of a three-digit gain, the bet loses money on average.

bloecke.md:
## Hit rate and size of outcomes

The [[expected value]] is a product of two factors that can be changed separately. The concept of the asymmetric bet is based on this. What you are looking for is the decision in which the winning outcome is much larger than the losing outcome. That need not be the decision that is right most often. If you call the ratio of possible gain to possible loss the reward-to-risk ratio and measure both in multiples of the amount at risk, then the expected value per stake is

`E = p × reward-to-risk ratio − (1 − p)`

If you set E to zero and solve for p, you get the hit rate above which a bet is worthwhile: `p = 1 / (1 + reward-to-risk ratio)`. It follows that a strategy with 70% hits can be ruinous and one with 25% hits can pay off. The hit rate alone is therefore not meaningful.

bloecke.titel: Required hit rate by reward-to-risk ratio

bloecke.md: The statement “I was right in eight out of ten cases” is not meaningful without the size of the outcomes. Conversely, the same applies to “this could increase tenfold” as long as no probability is given. A statement about a bet that gives only one of the two numbers is incomplete. Usually the second number is missing on purpose.

## The base rate as a starting point

Before assessing how good an individual case is, you ask how well cases of this kind perform on average. This prior frequency is called the [[base rate (statistics)|base rate]]. It is publicly available, but is almost always ignored, because it remains abstract and the individual story is more vivid. Such individual stories are, for example, about the manager with the clear thesis, the start-up with the good product or the share with the convincing narrative.

For the question of whether an actively managed fund can beat its index, the base rate has been available as a statistic for years. S&P Dow Jones Indices measures every six months how many active funds miss their category benchmark. Funds that were closed or merged during the period are also included. For funds denominated in euros, the success rates as of 30 June 2025 are low.

bloecke.titel: Share of active funds that beat their benchmark over ten years
bloecke.unter: SPIVA Europe Mid-Year 2025, funds in euros, as of 30 Jun 2025. The largest category, global equity funds, has the lowest rate.

bloecke.md:
## Conditional probability and inferences

Most misjudgements arise with conditional probability. You observe an outcome and infer the cause from it. Such outcomes are, for example, three good years, a very good balance sheet or a series of correct forecasts. The question, however, is how likely skill is, given the outcome. That is something different from the probability with which genuine skill leads to this outcome. They are two different numbers, and [[Bayes' theorem]] converts one into the other.

bloecke.erklaerung: In practice, it is easier to calculate with odds than with probabilities: odds after the evidence = odds before the evidence × (probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is true / probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is false). The fraction is called the likelihood ratio. It measures how well a piece of evidence distinguishes between a true and a false hypothesis. If it is close to 1, the evidence is worthless, even if it looks impressive.
variablen: Prior assumption before the evidence, that is, the base rate
How likely the evidence would be if the hypothesis is true

bloecke.titel: Three good years in a row
bloecke.md:
The illustrative calculation is based on deliberately generous assumptions. Of 100 fund managers, 10 are genuinely skilled. A skilled manager beats the benchmark in any single year with a probability of 65%, an unskilled one, after costs, with 45%. A manager has beaten the benchmark three years in a row.

- Of the 10 skilled managers, 10 × 0.65³ = 2.75 achieve the streak.
- Of the 90 unskilled managers, 90 × 0.45³ = 8.20 achieve the streak.
- In total, 10.95 managers have this streak, 2.75 of whom are skilled.

Among the managers with a streak, the share of skilled managers is therefore 2.75 / 10.95 = 25%. Three good years thus raise the assessment from 10% to 25%. Luck nevertheless remains three times as likely as skill as the explanation for the streak. The obvious conclusion that the manager is skilled confuses P(streak | skill) with P(skill | streak).

bloecke.titel: Probability of skill after consecutive good years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with an annual hit rate of 65% versus 45%. The prior assumption shifts the curve more than any single additional year. With a base rate of 2%, the probability of skill remains below the 50% mark even after ten good years.

bloecke.md: The error does not lie in overestimating the evidence. It consists in not forming the prior assumption in the first place. In practice, a league table shows the best funds of recent years, and the prior assumption “almost none stays at the top” is not taken into account, even though it has long been measured. Of the US equity funds that were in the top quartile in 2021, none remained in the top quartile in all four following years up to 2025, except among small-cap funds (around 2%). Pure chance would have produced 0.25⁴ = 0.39%.

## Distorted weighting of probabilities

The third building block is a bias that cannot be removed by argument. In Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, probability does not enter the evaluation unchanged. It is converted through [[probability weighting]], in which small probabilities are overweighted and medium and large ones underweighted. The frequently cited parameters of this function come from a single paper from 1992 and are difficult to verify. Qualitatively, the finding is robust. It also explains four behaviours that would otherwise seem to contradict each other.

bloecke.unter: The same person behaves in a risk-seeking or risk-averse way depending on the quadrant. This is due to the distorted perception of probability, not to their character.
bloecke.yLabel: Gains at the top, losses at the bottom

felder.text: The small chance of winning is overweighted. You pay more for the jackpot than it is worth, and for the same reason buy the share with the big story.
The high chance of winning is underweighted. The sure smaller gain seems more attractive, and the winner is sold too early.
The small probability of loss is overweighted. You willingly pay a premium above the expected value. Sensible for losses that threaten your livelihood, expensive for minor losses.
The high probability of loss is underweighted. You prefer the small chance of no loss to the sure smaller loss. This explains holding on to losers.

bloecke.titel: Expected value in games of chance
bloecke.md: In games of chance, nobody has to estimate the expected value, because the amount withheld is set out in the rules. The chance of six correct numbers in Lotto 6aus49 is 1 in 13,983,816, and 1 in 139,838,160 with the Superzahl (an additional digit from 0 to 9). These values follow exactly from combinatorics. Around half of the stakes are paid out. The lottery tax under Section 26 RennwLottG (Racing Betting and Lottery Act) of 20% of the participation fee (ticket price including the operator's fees) excluding tax (Sections 27 and 29 RennwLottG) is included in the stake. Like the levies for charitable purposes and the operator's costs, it is paid out of the other half and does not reduce the expected value any further. The winnings themselves remain tax-free for the player, because they do not fall under any of the seven types of income in Section 2(1) EStG (Income Tax Act). Income from later investing the winnings, by contrast, is taxable like other capital income.

zeilen: Around half of the stakes are paid out; lottery tax (Section 26 RennwLottG), levies and costs are paid from the other half
Around 5% sports betting tax on the stake (5.3% of the stake excluding tax, Sections 17 and 18 RennwLottG), plus the bookmaker's margin
Broadly diversified equity portfolio, one year
No operator takes anything, the companies generate profits
Positive, amount cannot be reliably quantified

bloecke.md:
The first three rows differ fundamentally from the fourth. Lottery, betting and roulette are negative-sum games. The operator takes a fixed share in advance, so the participants inevitably distribute less among themselves afterwards than they staked. A stock market also redistributes, but in addition passes the companies' profits on to their owners. The statement “the stock market is just gambling too” confuses the structure of the game with the fluctuation of the outcomes. This difference says nothing about the level of equity returns, but it does say something about the sign of the expected value.

## Expected value after tax

German tax law changes asymmetric bets, because it does not treat gains and losses symmetrically. Capital income is subject to flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% (Section 32d(1) EStG); with the solidarity surcharge it is 26.375%, plus church tax where applicable. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG). Gains are therefore reliably reduced. A loss, on the other hand, only has an effect if it is matched by suitable gains in the same year or a later one. For individual shares, only gains from share sales count for this, because Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG prescribes a separate offsetting group for share losses.

bloecke.titel: Worked example with flat-rate withholding tax
bloecke.md:
A position has two equally likely outcomes, +40% or −20%. Before tax, the expected value is 0.5 × 40 + 0.5 × (−20) = +10%.

- The gain is taxed and falls to 40 × (1 − 0.26375) = 29.45%.
- If the loss can be offset, it only counts at 20 × 0.73625 = 14.73%. The expected value is then 0.5 × 29.45 − 0.5 × 14.73 = +7.36%.
- If there are no suitable gains, the loss remains in full. The expected value is then 0.5 × 29.45 − 0.5 × 20 = +4.73%.

The same pre-tax advantage therefore falls to three quarters or to half, depending on the offsetting situation. For an equity ETF held as private assets, the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) mitigates the effect. The effective tax rate then falls to 18.46%, and losses are recorded in the general loss offset pot rather than in the narrower share loss pot.

bloecke.titel: From gross to net expected value
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for the position from the example above, in percentage points. The tax reduces the gain in every case. Whether it also reduces the loss depends on the loss offset pots.

bloecke.md:
- Translate every probability statement into frequencies, that is, “about 30 out of 100 cases like this one” instead of “good chances”.
- Look for the base rate before assessing any individual case. For almost every investment question, there is a public statistic that provides it.
- For every piece of evidence, check how often it would also occur if your own hypothesis were wrong. If it then occurs almost as often, the evidence is worthless.
- Write down forecasts as a range with a 90% interval, then double the range and check after twelve months. Experience shows that your own hit rate turns out worse than expected.

The expected value describes the average over many parallel paths. A single investor, however, only experiences one path, in which the outcomes multiply instead of adding up. That is why a bet can have a clearly positive expected value and still be certain to ruin an investor who takes it repeatedly. In practice, you therefore rule out ruin first and only then optimise the expected value. The difference between the ensemble average and the time average is the topic of the next lesson.

mitnehmen: The expected value is always a product of probability and size, so a statement with only one of the two numbers is not meaningful.
The required hit rate falls as the reward-to-risk ratio rises, according to p = 1 / (1 + reward-to-risk ratio), so that with a ratio of 3:1, 25% hits are already enough.
The base rate comes before the assessment of an individual case; over ten years, for example, only 1.78% of active global equity funds in euros beat their benchmark.
Bayes' theorem converts the probability of an outcome given skill into the probability you are looking for, that of skill given this outcome.
Small probabilities are overweighted and large ones underweighted, which leads to lottery behaviour, taking gains too early and sitting out losses.
After tax, a symmetrical bet is no longer symmetrical, because the gain is certain to be reduced and the loss only counts if it can be offset.

begriffe.text: The sum of all possible outcomes of a decision, weighted by their probabilities. It describes an average over many repetitions and is not a forecast for the individual case.

The frequency of an outcome in the population before characteristics of the individual case are taken into account. It is the starting point of every probability estimate and is usually passed over in favour of the more vivid individual story.

Rule by which a probability is updated when new evidence becomes available. It combines the base rate with the strength of the evidence and converts P(evidence given hypothesis) into P(hypothesis given evidence).
Ratio of the possible gain to the possible loss of a position. It determines the hit rate above which a bet pays off: p = 1 / (1 + reward-to-risk ratio).
Component of prospect theory according to which people do not translate probabilities into decisions linearly. They overweight small probabilities and underweight medium to large ones.
